angle.point: A tiny blip on a new monitor, which a young astronomer refused to wave away, turned seventeen years of fake space signals into a kitchen microwave, and that is how fast radio bursts were shown to be real.
angle.stakes: Emily Petroff was a PhD student hunting fast radio bursts from deep space; the look-alike 'perytons' at Parkes had made people doubt whether those bursts were real at all, so the thing she was chasing could have turned out to be local noise.
angle.turn: The new interference monitor showed every peryton came with a blip on the same band microwave ovens use, and opening the staff kitchen microwave before the timer finished made a peryton on cue.
angle.takeaway: One true story where a strange little detail (a lunchtime blip) turned out to matter, and how people actually worked it out: by checking it, in the kitchen, with a mug of water.

beats.speaker: ori
beats.voiceover: Since 1998, the Parkes radio dish in Australia kept catching quick, strange bursts called perytons. They looked a lot like fast radio bursts from deep space, but they showed up in office hours, mostly around lunchtime.

beats.speaker: ori
beats.voiceover: Emily Petroff, a PhD student hunting the real bursts, needed to know if they were just local noise too. In January 2015, a new radio monitor caught three perytons, and each one came with a blip on the band microwave ovens use. So her team ran the staff kitchen microwave and opened the door before the timer finished. The dish caught a peryton, right on cue.

beats.speaker: ori
beats.voiceover: Here's the footnote. A microwave couldn't have made the very first fast radio burst, so those bursts were real, and today they're traced to other galaxies.

beats.speaker: ori
beats.voiceover: Seventeen years of strange bursts, and the answer was a microwave door opened too soon.

claims.claim: Perytons at the Parkes radio telescope were caused by on-site microwave ovens, and they clustered around lunchtime (hook: 'Lunch fooled a telescope'; also the title bar).
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, 'Identifying the source of perytons at the Parkes radio telescope', MNRAS 451, 3933; arXiv:1504.02165 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.02165), section on relevance to FRBs: 'the clustering around the lunchtime hour'
claims.note: 'Fooled' = the signals mimicked an astrophysical pulse closely enough to cast doubt on the first FRB.

claims.claim: Perytons have been detected at Parkes since 1998 (46 of them by 2015, 16 on 23 June 1998).
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165, section 'The Peryton Cluster of 23rd June 1998': 'Of the 46 perytons detected at Parkes since 1998…'

claims.claim: Parkes is a radio dish (radio telescope) in Australia.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165 (Parkes radio telescope, with the Australia Telescope Compact Array 400 km north of Parkes); Swinburne University news, May 2015 ('The Dish')

claims.claim: Perytons are millisecond-long bursts whose frequency sweep mimics an astrophysical pulse, and their similarity to the first fast radio burst (FRB 010724) cast doubt on FRBs being from deep space.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165, abstract: 'their similarity to FRB 010724 had cast doubt on the interpretation of FRBs as extragalactic'

claims.claim: Perytons occurred during office hours, clustered around lunchtime.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165 (time-of-day distribution, Figure 7: clustered in office hours, 'particularly around lunch time'); Swinburne University, 'How we found the source of the mystery signals at The Dish' (May 2015), https://www.swinburne.edu.au/news/2015/05/how-we-found-the-source-of-the-mystery-signals-at-the-dish

claims.claim: Emily Petroff was a PhD student (Swinburne University of Technology) working on fast radio bursts, and led the peryton study.
claims.source: Swinburne University news, May 2015 (byline: 'PhD candidate in Astro Physics at Swinburne University of Technology'), https://www.swinburne.edu.au/news/2015/05/how-we-found-the-source-of-the-mystery-signals-at-the-dish ; Petroff et al. 2015 (lead author; SUPERB survey searching for pulsars and FRBs)
claims.note: 'Needed to know if they were just local noise too' paraphrases the paper's stated aim: to address whether perytons and FRBs could have a common origin.

claims.claim: In January 2015 (the week of 19 January) three perytons were detected, and a newly installed RFI monitor (December 2014) showed each came with emission at 2.3–2.5 GHz, the band microwave ovens emit in.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165, sections 2–3 and Conclusions: 'In December 2014 an RFI monitoring system was installed on the Parkes site'; 'Three peryton detections… during the week of 19 January, 2015'; 'As microwave ovens are known to emit in this frequency range'
claims.note: Spoken as 'a new radio monitor'. Microwave ovens operate at about 2.45 GHz.

claims.claim: On 17 March 2015 the team ran the staff kitchen microwave and stopped it by opening the door before the cycle finished, producing perytons at the exact times the door was opened.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165, section 3: 'The decisive test occurred on 17 March, 2015… instead of waiting for the microwave cycle to finish the microwave was stopped by opening the door. This test produced 3 bright perytons from the staff kitchen microwave all at the exact times of opening the microwave oven door'
claims.note: 'Right on cue' = at the exact time of the door opening; the paper notes about a 50% success rate overall.

claims.claim: On-site microwaves could not have produced the first fast radio burst (FRB 010724), and FRBs remained strong candidates for genuine extragalactic signals.
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165, abstract: 'microwaves on site could not have caused FRB 010724… FRBs are strong candidates for genuine extragalactic transients'

claims.claim: Fast radio bursts have since been traced (localised) to host galaxies beyond the Milky Way.
claims.source: Chatterjee et al. 2017, 'A direct localization of a fast radio burst and its host', Nature 541, 58–61, doi:10.1038/nature20797

claims.claim: About seventeen years passed from the 1998 peryton detections to the 2015 microwave explanation (the '17 years' calendar).
claims.source: Petroff et al. 2015, arXiv:1504.02165 (perytons detected since 1998; source identified March 2015)

publish.title: Lunch fooled a telescope
publish.description: For seventeen years, Australia's Parkes radio dish caught strange bursts that looked like they came from deep space. In 2015 the answer turned up in the staff kitchen.
